mcqs.question: You run 10 app servers each enforcing a local, in-memory limit of 100 requests/minute per client. What is the actual effective limit a single client can reach?
options: Up to roughly 1,000 requests/minute if traffic is spread across all 10 nodes, since no node sees the client's total
Exactly 100 requests/minute, since the limit value itself doesn't change
Exactly 10 requests/minute, since each node divides the limit among itself
Unlimited, because per-node limiting doesn't work at all
mcqs.explanation: Each node only sees the fraction of requests routed to it, so a client hitting all 10 nodes can total up to 10x the per-node limit before any single node objects. The limit value is unchanged per node, but the effective global cap rises with node count — the core failure this topic addresses.

mcqs.question: Why does a naive "read counter, compare to limit, write counter" implementation across multiple nodes let more requests through than the configured limit?
options: Redis doesn't support increment operations, so the count is always approximate
Two nodes can both read the same pre-increment value and both proceed, since the read-check-write isn't atomic across them
The limit configuration itself gets corrupted under concurrent access
Network latency to Redis always rounds the count down
mcqs.explanation: The race is a classic check-then-act problem: without atomicity, two concurrent reads can both see room under the limit and both write an increment, letting one extra request through. Redis does support atomic INCR; the limit config isn't corrupted, and latency doesn't systematically round anything.

mcqs.question: A billing system enforces a hard monthly API quota tied to a customer's paid plan. Which limiting approach fits, and why?
options: Approximate local limiting, because it adds no latency
Per-node in-memory limiting, because it's the simplest to deploy
Strict centralized limiting, because any overage directly costs the business money and must be exact
No limiting at all, since billing is handled separately
mcqs.explanation: A billing-tied quota can't tolerate the brief overage that eventually-consistent approximate limiting allows, so the exactness of strict centralized checks is worth the added round trip. Per-node limiting doesn't produce one true global count, and skipping limiting entirely ignores the requirement altogether.

mcqs.question: After centralizing rate limiting in a single Redis instance checked on every request, the team keeps adding app servers to handle growth. What risk does this introduce?
options: None — centralizing in Redis removes any further scaling concern
The app servers will silently stop enforcing the limit
Redis itself can become the new shared bottleneck, since every added node adds more synchronous calls to the same instance
The rate limit will automatically increase to match the new node count
mcqs.explanation: Every app node makes a synchronous call to the same Redis instance, so scaling app servers scales load on Redis too, recreating the exact single-point-of-overload problem the limiter exists to prevent. The limit doesn't silently change or stop being enforced — the shared dependency just gets overloaded.
